title: CORS: Why Is the Browser Blocking Me?
description: Work through how browsers handle origins, CORS, preflights, credentials, opaque responses, SameSite cookies, CSP, CSRF, and the classic "but it works in Postman" trap.

questions.title: Are these two URLs same-origin?

options.text: Yes, because scheme and host match
No, because the ports differ
Yes, because both connections use TLS
It depends on the URL paths

questions.explanation: An origin is defined by its scheme, host, and port. The page uses the default HTTPS port, but the API uses port `8443`. Different ports mean different origins. The path does not matter.

questions.title: How are `https://app.example.com` and `https://api.example.com` related?

options.text: They are same-origin and same-site
They are cross-origin but same-site
They are cross-site because the subdomains differ
They become same-origin if both return CORS headers

questions.explanation: The URLs are cross-origin because their hosts differ. They are still same-site because they share the HTTPS scheme and the registrable domain `example.com`. CORS may let JavaScript read a cross-origin response, but it does not make the origins equal. Cookie rules and CORS can therefore reach different decisions.

questions.title: What does CORS control?

options.text: It lets a server say which origins may read a response through browser JavaScript
It lets a server approve methods and headers that ordinary HTML forms cannot send
It is a general server firewall that blocks non-browser HTTP clients
It guarantees that a rejected cross-origin request never reaches application code

questions.explanation: Browsers use CORS to decide whether JavaScript may read a cross-origin response. For requests with non-safelisted methods or headers, the browser first asks the server for permission with a preflight. CORS is not authentication or a firewall. Non-browser clients do not have to enforce it, and a safelisted request may reach the server even when JavaScript cannot read the response.

questions.title: A form-style cross-origin POST changes server state, but the response has no CORS headers. What happens?
questions.description: Assume the request uses `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded` and no non-safelisted headers.

images.alt: Two sequence diagrams comparing a simple cross-origin request, which goes straight to the server and only gates whether JavaScript may read the response, against a preflighted request, where the browser first sends an OPTIONS request asking permission, then sends the real request once permission is granted, and that real response still needs its own CORS headers to be readable.
images.caption: The top diagram — the request always goes out; CORS only decides whether JS can read what comes back.

options.text: The browser must preflight, so the POST is never sent
The POST can be sent and mutate state, but JavaScript cannot read the response
The browser rewrites the POST to GET
The response becomes readable as an opaque JSON object

questions.explanation: This POST is safelisted, so the browser can send it without a preflight. CORS controls whether JavaScript may read the response. It cannot undo work that the server has already performed. CORS alone therefore does not stop CSRF; an attacker may care only that the state changed.
questions.references:
- [WHATWG Fetch: CORS protocol](https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#cors-protocol)
- [OWASP: CSRF Prevention, disallowing simple requests](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Cross-Site_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html#disallowing-simple-requests)

questions.title: Which changes would trigger a CORS preflight?
questions.description: Start with a cross-origin `GET` that has no custom headers. Each correct change triggers a preflight on its own.

options.text: Change the method to `PUT`
Add `Authorization: Bearer token`
Change it to a POST with `Content-Type: application/json`
Add `X-Trace-Id: 42`
Add an ordinary `Accept: application/json` header

questions.explanation: The safelisted methods are `GET`, `HEAD`, and `POST`. `Authorization` and custom `X-*` headers are not safelisted. A safelisted `Content-Type` must be `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, `multipart/form-data`, or `text/plain`; `application/json` does not qualify. A normal `Accept: application/json` header is safelisted.

questions.title: Which cross-origin requests can avoid a CORS preflight?
questions.description: Assume every header value meets the CORS safelist limits.

images.alt: Two sequence diagrams comparing a simple cross-origin request, which goes straight to the server and only gates whether JavaScript may read the response, against a preflighted request, where the browser first sends an OPTIONS request asking permission, then sends the real request once permission is granted, and that real response still needs its own CORS headers to be readable.
images.caption: The top diagram's single GET — no OPTIONS round trip before it.

options.text: `GET` with `Accept: application/json`
`POST` with `Content-Type: multipart/form-data` set by the browser for `FormData`
`DELETE` with no body
`POST` with `Content-Type: application/json` and an empty body
`GET` with `X-Requested-With: XMLHttpRequest`

questions.explanation: The browser looks at the method and headers, not whether the body is empty. A `GET` with a safelisted `Accept` value qualifies. So does a `FormData` POST when the browser sets `Content-Type`. `DELETE`, `application/json`, and `X-Requested-With` each trigger a preflight.

questions.title: Which request matches the preflight for a `PATCH` with `Content-Type` and `X-Trace-Id`?

images.alt: Two sequence diagrams comparing a simple cross-origin request, which goes straight to the server and only gates whether JavaScript may read the response, against a preflighted request, where the browser first sends an OPTIONS request asking permission, then sends the real request once permission is granted, and that real response still needs its own CORS headers to be readable.
images.caption: The bottom diagram's first arrow — the exact OPTIONS request this question describes.

options.text: An `OPTIONS` request with `Origin`, `Access-Control-Request-Method: PATCH`, and `Access-Control-Request-Headers` naming the non-safelisted headers
A `HEAD` request containing the future PATCH body
A `PATCH` request with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` set by the browser
An `OPTIONS` request with `Access-Control-Allow-Methods: PATCH` supplied by the browser

questions.explanation: The browser sends an `OPTIONS` request with `Origin` and `Access-Control-Request-Method`. It also sends `Access-Control-Request-Headers` when the planned request has non-safelisted headers. The server puts the `Access-Control-Allow-*` headers on its response.

questions.title: Will a CORS preflight include the user's session cookie?

images.alt: Two sequence diagrams comparing a simple cross-origin request, which goes straight to the server and only gates whether JavaScript may read the response, against a preflighted request, where the browser first sends an OPTIONS request asking permission, then sends the real request once permission is granted, and that real response still needs its own CORS headers to be readable.
images.caption: The note under the bottom diagram's second arrow — the preflight's credentials mode is always same-origin.

options.text: Yes, whenever the future request uses `credentials: "include"`
No. A cross-origin CORS preflight excludes credentials
Only if `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` was cached
Only for same-site cross-origin requests

questions.explanation: A preflight always uses credentials mode `same-origin`. On a cross-origin request, that excludes cookies and HTTP authentication. The actual request may carry credentials later if CORS, Fetch, cookie rules, and browser policy all allow it. Middleware that requires a session for `OPTIONS` often blocks valid preflights.

questions.title: Can `204 No Content` be a successful preflight response?

options.text: Yes. Any successful 2xx status works if the required CORS headers match
No, every preflight must return `200` with a JSON body
Only when the actual request is a `GET`
Only when `Access-Control-Max-Age` is zero

questions.explanation: A preflight needs a successful 2xx status and matching CORS headers. Both `200` and `204` work, and the browser does not require a response body. A `200` HTML login page still fails if its CORS headers are missing or wrong.

questions.title: Your auth middleware returns `401` for every unauthenticated `OPTIONS` request. How should you fix it?
questions.description: The later credentialed API request is legitimate, but its browser preflight never succeeds.

options.text: Handle the preflight before session authentication, then authenticate the actual request
Copy the session token into JavaScript and add it as a query parameter to `OPTIONS`
Switch the actual request to `mode: "no-cors"`
Return `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` from the `401` response and keep requiring the session cookie

questions.explanation: A cross-origin preflight has no session credentials, so session middleware cannot authenticate it. Check the requested origin, method, and headers when handling `OPTIONS`. Then apply normal authentication and authorization to the actual state-changing request.

questions.title: A preflight succeeds, then the actual `PATCH` returns `500` without `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`. What can browser JavaScript observe?

images.alt: Two sequence diagrams comparing a simple cross-origin request, which goes straight to the server and only gates whether JavaScript may read the response, against a preflighted request, where the browser first sends an OPTIONS request asking permission, then sends the real request once permission is granted, and that real response still needs its own CORS headers to be readable.
images.caption: The bottom diagram's last arrow and the callout below it — exactly this scenario.

options.text: The full `500` body, because the preflight already granted access
A CORS failure rather than the readable error response
A synthetic `204` generated from the cached preflight
The body is readable only if it is JSON

questions.explanation: A successful preflight allows the browser to send the `PATCH`. The actual response still has to pass its own CORS check. If browser code should read an error response, the server must add the right CORS headers to that response too.

questions.title: Why might clearing the normal HTTP cache leave a preflight result cached?

options.text: The browser keeps preflight results in a separate CORS-preflight cache
Preflight responses are permanently stored in IndexedDB
Service workers are required to retain every `OPTIONS` response
`OPTIONS` responses are never cached anywhere

questions.explanation: The CORS-preflight cache is separate from the normal HTTP cache. Its entries depend on the network partition key, request origin, URL, credentials mode, method, and header name. `Access-Control-Max-Age` sets a lifetime, but browsers may cap it or remove an entry early.

questions.title: Why does `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` fail for `fetch(url, { credentials: "include" })`?

options.text: A credentialed response must name the requesting origin explicitly
The wildcard is valid only for `POST` requests
The wildcard is a request header, not a response header
Credentials can never be used in cross-origin requests

questions.explanation: When credentials mode is `include`, `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` fails the CORS check. The server must return the exact requesting origin and `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. A wildcard would otherwise expose user-specific responses to every origin.

questions.title: Which response header pair can share a credentialed response with a page at `https://app.example.com`?

options.text: `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com` and `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`
`Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` and `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`
`Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com/` and `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: yes`
`Origin: https://app.example.com` and `Credentials: include`

questions.explanation: The allowed origin must match the serialized origin, which has no trailing slash. `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials` requires the case-sensitive value `true`. The browser sends `Origin` as a request header. `credentials: "include"` is a Fetch option, not a response header.

questions.title: Will `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: True` authorize a credentialed CORS response?

options.text: No. The required value is the case-sensitive byte sequence `true`
Yes. All HTTP field values are case-insensitive
Yes, but only over HTTPS
No. The required value is `1`

questions.explanation: The CORS grammar requires the exact value `true`. The Fetch Standard even lists `True` as a failing example. Header names are case-insensitive, but this header value is not.

questions.title: Is `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://a.example, https://b.example` a valid two-origin allowlist?

options.text: No. The field accepts one serialized origin, `null`, or `*`
Yes, because all HTTP response fields accept comma-separated lists
Yes, but only for requests without credentials
No. Only one origin may ever use an API deployment

questions.explanation: `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` accepts one origin, `null`, or `*`. To support several trusted origins, compare the request's `Origin` with an allowlist and return the one matching origin. Do not put the full allowlist in the header.

questions.title: Which cache header should you send when `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` changes with the request's `Origin`?

options.text: `Vary: Origin`
`Cache-Control: cors`
`Access-Control-Max-Age: Origin`
`ETag: Origin`

questions.explanation: `Vary: Origin` tells caches that the response depends on the incoming `Origin`. Without it, a cached response prepared for one origin may be reused for another. Fetch recommends `Vary` when the policy is more complex than an always-sent wildcard or one static origin.

questions.title: Why is it dangerous to copy any request `Origin` into `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` when credentials are enabled?

options.text: It lets any attacker-controlled origin read user-specific responses
It prevents the browser from sending the `Origin` header
It forces every request to use `mode: "no-cors"`
It changes the API server's own origin

questions.explanation: Only echo an origin after it passes an exact allowlist check. If credentials are allowed, blind reflection lets an attacker's site read responses sent with the victim's ambient credentials. This creates the confused-deputy risk described by Fetch.

questions.title: What is the default `credentials` mode for `fetch("https://api.other.example/data")`?

options.text: `same-origin`
`include`
`omit`
It is inherited from `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials`

questions.explanation: A Fetch request created from a URL string defaults to `same-origin`. It includes credentials for same-origin URLs, but not for cross-origin URLs. A response header cannot change the mode after the request was sent. Client code must request cross-origin credentials, and the other security checks must still allow them.

questions.title: What does `credentials: "include"` guarantee for a cross-site cookie?

options.text: It allows credentials, but cookie matching, SameSite, Secure, expiry, and browser policy still apply
It sends every cookie in the browser, regardless of domain
It overrides `SameSite=Lax` and third-party cookie blocking
It converts an `HttpOnly` cookie into an `Authorization` header

questions.explanation: The Fetch setting allows credentials to be used. The browser still checks the cookie's host or domain, path, expiry, `Secure`, `SameSite`, and its own cookie policy. `include` does not override those checks.

questions.title: Can the browser accept `Set-Cookie` even when CORS prevents JavaScript from reading the response?
questions.description: Assume the request uses `credentials: "include"` and the cookie passes the SameSite, Secure, domain, and browser-policy checks.

options.text: Yes. The CORS check can fail while the browser still processes `Set-Cookie`
No. CORS failure rolls back all network and cookie effects
Only if JavaScript reads the `Set-Cookie` response header
Only if the server returns `Access-Control-Expose-Headers: Set-Cookie`

questions.explanation: CORS controls whether JavaScript may read the response. It does not roll back network or cookie effects. Fetch notes that `Set-Cookie` may still be honored when the response fails the CORS sharing check. The normal cookie rules and browser policy still apply.

questions.title: Does `Access-Control-Allow-Headers: *` allow an `Authorization` request header?

options.text: No. The server must list `Authorization` explicitly
Yes. `*` always matches every request header in CORS
Yes, but only when the token begins with `Bearer`
No. Browsers forbid JavaScript from setting `Authorization` under all circumstances

questions.explanation: Fetch treats `Authorization` as a non-wildcard request header. The server must name it in `Access-Control-Allow-Headers`. That only lets the browser send the header; the server must still validate the token on the actual request.

questions.title: The Network panel shows `X-Request-Id: abc`, but `response.headers.get("X-Request-Id")` returns `null`. What is missing?

options.text: `Access-Control-Expose-Headers: X-Request-Id` on the response
`Access-Control-Allow-Headers: X-Request-Id` on the response
`Access-Control-Request-Headers: X-Request-Id` on the actual request
`Vary: X-Request-Id` on the request

questions.explanation: `Access-Control-Allow-Headers` approves non-safelisted request headers during preflight. `Access-Control-Expose-Headers` names extra response headers that JavaScript may read. DevTools can show network headers that page code cannot access.

questions.title: Can frontend JavaScript read `Set-Cookie` by asking the server to send `Access-Control-Expose-Headers: Set-Cookie`?

options.text: No. `Set-Cookie` is a forbidden response header and stays hidden from frontend JavaScript
Yes, provided the request uses `credentials: "include"`
Yes, but only for a cookie without `HttpOnly`
Yes, if `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` names the exact origin

questions.explanation: Fetch marks `Set-Cookie` and `Set-Cookie2` as forbidden response headers. `Access-Control-Expose-Headers` cannot make them appear in `Response.headers`. The browser handles eligible cookies itself, so frontend code should not try to parse `Set-Cookie`.

questions.title: What numeric `status` does JavaScript observe on an opaque response?
questions.description: Enter the status number defined by Fetch.
questions.explanation: JavaScript sees status `0`, an empty status message, no headers, and no readable body. The browser hides the internal response so thoroughly that an opaque response looks much like a network error to page code.

questions.title: What can JavaScript read from a successful cross-origin JSON response fetched with `mode: "no-cors"`?

options.text: It returns an opaque response whose body and most metadata are unavailable to JavaScript
It disables CORS and exposes the JSON normally
It proxies the request through the page's own origin
It converts the response into a same-origin response

questions.explanation: For a cross-origin fetch, `no-cors` produces an opaque response. Code cannot inspect its JSON, status, or headers. Use this mode only when the caller does not need to read the response, such as in some fire-and-forget or caching flows.

questions.title: Can a `no-cors` request have server-side effects even though JavaScript receives an opaque response?

options.text: Yes. Opacity hides the response but does not stop the server from processing the request
No. Opaque means the browser never sent any bytes
Only if the opaque response reports `ok: true`
Only if the server also returns `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`

questions.explanation: Opacity describes what JavaScript can see. The browser can still send the request, and the server can still perform work. Since the response exposes status `0` and no body, client code cannot use it to confirm success.

questions.title: Why can't a rejected `fetch()` promise reliably distinguish a CORS failure from a network failure?

options.text: Fetch represents a failed CORS check as a network error and rejects with limited detail
JavaScript promises erase all Error objects
CORS failures always return HTTP `418`
DNS failures are converted into opaque responses

questions.explanation: Fetch turns a failed CORS check into a network error so it does not leak response details. Page code often gets only a generic error such as `TypeError: Failed to fetch`. Check the browser Console and Network panel, then compare the preflight, actual response, and server logs.

questions.title: What does "it works in the Postman desktop app" prove about a browser CORS failure?

options.text: Postman can reach the endpoint, but the browser may still block the page from sending the request or reading the response
It proves the server's CORS headers are correct
It proves the browser has a corrupted HTTP cache
It proves cookies and CSP behave identically in both clients

questions.explanation: The Postman desktop app is not running inside the page's browser security context. It can send requests without browser CORS limits. Success there proves that Postman reached the endpoint and received a response. It does not prove that a browser preflight, cookies, response exposure, or the page's CSP will behave as needed.

questions.title: Will a `SameSite=Lax` session cookie accompany a cross-site `fetch()` POST from another site?

options.text: No. The Lax exception covers certain top-level navigations with safe methods, not a cross-site fetch POST
Yes, whenever Fetch uses `credentials: "include"`
Yes, because POST is a safe HTTP method
Only when `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` is on the request

questions.explanation: A cross-site fetch is not a top-level navigation, and POST is not a safe method. `credentials: "include"` does not override `SameSite`. The CORS setup may be correct while the API still sees an unauthenticated request because the browser left out the cookie.

questions.title: When can a `SameSite=Lax` cookie be sent from a cross-site context?

options.text: On a top-level navigation that uses a safe method, such as following a normal GET link
On every cross-site iframe request
On any cross-site POST if the response is JSON
Only after a successful CORS preflight

questions.explanation: Lax allows cookies on certain cross-site top-level navigations that use safe methods. A normal GET link can therefore keep the user signed in, while an embedded cross-site fetch does not receive the same cookie.

questions.title: What happens to `Set-Cookie: session=abc; SameSite=None` when the `Secure` attribute is absent?

options.text: The browser ignores it because `SameSite=None` requires `Secure`
The cookie is stored and treated as `SameSite=Lax`
The cookie is stored but becomes `HttpOnly` automatically
The cookie is accepted whenever CORS allows credentials

questions.explanation: The browser rejects a `SameSite=None` cookie unless it also has `Secure`. A cross-site session cookie therefore usually needs `SameSite=None; Secure`. Its domain and path must still match, and browser policy must allow the cookie.

questions.title: A page on `https://app.example.com` fetches `https://api.example.com`. Which statements are true?

options.text: A SameSite cookie can be eligible because the request is same-site
CORS can still be required because the request is cross-origin
Same-site status makes the hosts same-origin
Successful CORS automatically makes every domain cookie eligible

questions.explanation: Same-site and same-origin are different checks. These HTTPS subdomains are same-site, so a matching cookie may be eligible. Their hosts differ, which makes them cross-origin. JavaScript still needs CORS permission to read the response.

questions.title: Can a browser withhold a cross-site cookie even when Fetch, SameSite, Secure, and CORS are configured correctly?

options.text: Yes. The browser's third-party cookie policy can add more restrictions
No. Those settings force every conforming browser to send it
Only if the preflight status is `204`
Only if the response omits `Content-Type`

questions.explanation: The cookie specification allows browsers to restrict third-party cookies. Fetch and CORS settings do not override privacy controls, user settings, cookie partitioning, or blocking policies. Sites cannot assume every browser treats third-party cookies the same way.

questions.title: What protection does `HttpOnly` provide for a session cookie?

options.text: It hides the cookie from APIs such as `document.cookie`, but eligible HTTP requests can still send it
It prevents the browser from ever sending the cookie cross-origin
It makes the cookie same-origin instead of same-site
It replaces the need for `Secure` and `SameSite`

questions.explanation: `HttpOnly` blocks access through non-HTTP APIs such as `document.cookie`. It does not stop the browser from sending the cookie on an eligible HTTP request. Domain, path, `Secure`, `SameSite`, credentials mode, and browser policy still apply. These attributes solve different problems and can be combined.

questions.title: Why do cookie-authenticated endpoints still need CSRF protection when their CORS policy is strict?

options.text: Cross-site requests can sometimes be sent without preflight, and an attacker may need only the side effect rather than the response
CORS applies only to GET and never to POST
CSRF is possible only when JavaScript can read `Set-Cookie`
A CSRF token is a replacement for server-side authorization

questions.explanation: Browsers can send form-compatible cross-site requests with ambient cookies. The attacker may not be able to read the response, but a vulnerable endpoint can still change state. Use CSRF tokens or Origin and Referer checks where appropriate. Keep safe methods free of side effects, and treat SameSite as another layer of protection.
questions.references:
- [IETF HTTPbis: Cookies and ambient authority](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis-22#section-8.2)
- [OWASP: CSRF Prevention Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Cross-Site_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html)

questions.title: Why does the page's inline script fail under `Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'self'`?

options.text: `'self'` allows script files from the page's origin, but not arbitrary inline scripts
CSP treats `startApp` as a cross-origin host name
Inline scripts are allowed only when CORS preflight succeeds
The script would run if the function returned JSON

questions.explanation: `'self'` allows matching script files from the page's origin. It does not allow inline code. An inline script needs a matching nonce or hash, or the much broader `'unsafe-inline'` permission. This block comes from CSP, not CORS.

questions.title: Which change allows this inline bootstrap script under CSP?
questions.description: The response policy contains `script-src 'nonce-r4nd0m'`, and the document contains `<script>startApp()</script>`.

options.text: Add `nonce="r4nd0m"` to that `script` element
Add `crossorigin="anonymous"` to that `script` element
Return `Access-Control-Allow-Nonce: r4nd0m` from every API
Add `SameSite=None` to the page's cookies

questions.explanation: The nonce in the `script` element must match the nonce in the policy. In production, the server should generate an unpredictable value for each response and put it in both the CSP header and every trusted inline script.
questions.references: [W3C CSP Level 3: Nonce sources and nonce reuse](https://www.w3.org/TR/CSP3/#security-nonce-reuse)

questions.title: Why should a CSP nonce not be a constant copied into every response?

options.text: An attacker who learns or predicts the nonce can run an injected script
Browsers permit a nonce to contain each character only once
A repeated nonce automatically changes the page's origin
CORS preflight caches reject repeated nonce strings

questions.explanation: A matching nonce allows the script despite the directive's other source restrictions. If an attacker can predict the nonce, it no longer proves that the script is trusted. CSP requires a new value for each policy and recommends at least 128 random bits from a cryptographically secure source.

questions.title: Why can one extra space break a CSP hash for an inline script?

options.text: The hash covers the script text, so changed whitespace produces a different digest
CSP forbids all whitespace inside inline scripts
Spaces cause the request to require a CORS preflight
The browser interprets any space as `'unsafe-inline'`

questions.explanation: A CSP hash matches the exact encoded script text. Even harmless whitespace changes the digest. If a build tool reformats inline code, it must also update the policy hash. Another option is to move the code out of the HTML.
questions.references: [W3C CSP Level 3: Element matching and hash sources](https://www.w3.org/TR/CSP3/#match-element-to-source-list)

questions.title: The API returns correct CORS headers, but the page has `Content-Security-Policy: connect-src 'self'`. Why does the fetch still fail?

options.text: The page's CSP blocks the connection before the API's CORS permission can help
`connect-src` changes the API response to `text/plain`
CORS headers are valid only when CSP is absent
`'self'` includes every HTTPS origin

questions.explanation: CSP and CORS are separate checks. The page's `connect-src` limits destinations for Fetch, XHR, WebSocket, EventSource, Beacon, and similar connections. If CSP blocks the destination, the API's CORS headers cannot make the request succeed.

questions.title: What does `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'` imply for a cross-origin `fetch()` when no `connect-src` is present?

options.text: `default-src` supplies the fallback source list, so the cross-origin connection is blocked
Nothing. `default-src` affects images only
The browser sends a CSP preflight to ask the API
The fetch is allowed if the API returns `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`

questions.explanation: When `connect-src` is missing, it falls back to `default-src`. Here that fallback is `'self'`, so CSP blocks the external API regardless of its CORS headers. An explicit `connect-src` would replace the fallback for these connections.

questions.title: How can you test a proposed CSP without enforcing it?

options.text: Send it as `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only` and monitor violations
Set `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` temporarily
Put `'unsafe-inline'` in every directive permanently
Test only with Postman because it evaluates page CSP

questions.explanation: A report-only policy records violations without blocking resources. You can use those reports to fix the policy before enforcing it. Reports can be noisy and may contain sensitive context, so store and review them carefully.

questions.title: Which limits apply when CSP is delivered through a `<meta>` element?

options.text: The policy does not apply to content that appears before the meta element
`Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only` is not supported through the meta mechanism
`frame-ancestors` and `sandbox` are not supported there
A meta policy can relax a stricter CSP response header

questions.explanation: A meta policy starts only after the browser processes the element. It cannot provide report-only mode, `report-uri`, `frame-ancestors`, or `sandbox`. If the response also has a CSP header, both policies apply. A meta policy cannot loosen the header policy.
questions.references:
- [W3C CSP Level 3: The meta element](https://www.w3.org/TR/CSP3/#meta-element)
- [W3C CSP Level 3: Multiple policies](https://www.w3.org/TR/CSP3/#multiple-policies)
